subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
For two years Elif and Vera had eaten lunch together at the kebab place near the office in Istanbul, every Wednesday. Since Elif became team lead in spring, she'd missed five in a row.
'Leads' lunch,' she texted the first time. After that, just 'busy'.
When Vera stopped by her desk to ask about the new release plan, Elif didn't look up. 'It's a leadership decision, Vera. You wouldn't really get the budget side.' Vera, who had worked on budgets longer than Elif, went quiet.
Some things Elif really couldn't share now: salaries, a colleague's performance review. That part was fair. But she also stopped telling Vera the small things, the jokes from meetings, the gossip about the new coffee machine.
On Friday, walking past the kebab place, she saw Vera there with two others from the old team, laughing. Elif felt a small sting, and then told herself she had outgrown that table anyway.

qa.q: How many Wednesday lunches in a row had Elif missed?
qa.a: She had missed five in a row.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when she saw Vera laughing with the old team?
qa.a: She felt a small sting of loneliness or exclusion, then covered it by telling herself she had outgrown them.

qa.q: What could Elif do to keep healthy distance without looking down on old friends?
qa.a: She could keep private matters private but still join some Wednesday lunches and speak to Vera as an equal.

qa.q: How does Vera experience Elif's comment about not getting the budget side?
qa.a: Vera feels talked down to and hurt, since Vera has actually worked on budgets longer than Elif.

grounding: It shows a new lead skipping lunches with an old friend, talking down to that friend and sharing less, mixing natural distance with a sense of being above the old team.

The staff room at Greenfields School still had the same cracked kettle, but Anand no longer drank tea there. Since he became head of the maths department in June, he took his lunch in the small HOD cabin with the door half shut.
Disha, who had shared a timetable and a table with him for four years, noticed first. At the department meeting on Tuesday she suggested moving the Class 9 test by a week.
'Let me explain it slowly,' Anand said, 'since you weren't in the planning meeting.' Two junior teachers glanced at each other.
He had also stopped forwarding the circulars. Disha found out about the new syllabus from the peon.
Some of it she understood. He had parent complaints to handle now, and things he couldn't discuss. But the way he said 'slowly' stayed with her the rest of the day.

qa.q: Where did Anand take his lunch after becoming head of the maths department?
qa.a: He took his lunch in the small HOD cabin with the door half shut.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling after Anand said 'Let me explain it slowly'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and belittled, since the remark stayed with her for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What could Anand change to keep a fair distance without seeming above his old colleagues?
qa.a: He could keep confidential matters private but still share circulars, speak to Disha as an equal, and sometimes eat in the staff room.

qa.q: How might the two junior teachers see Anand after the meeting?
qa.a: They may start to see him as someone who talks down to people, and feel less willing to speak up in front of him.

grounding: It shows a newly promoted head skipping the staff room, talking down to an old colleague and sharing less, beyond the natural distance of the role.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
It's been four months since I became lead, and I've stopped going to the Thursday lunch at the dhaba behind the office. I tell myself I'm busy, and I am. But I also didn't want to sit with Manjula and the others and hear them grumble about decisions I now make.
Last week Manjula asked me in the corridor why the deadline had moved. I said, "It's complicated, you don't need to worry about that level," and watched her face close. We used to share everything.
I've started keeping the planning notes to myself, too. Partly because I'm told to, and partly because it feels good to know things they don't.
Some distance comes with the job; I know that. But yesterday, walking past their table, I caught myself thinking they were small-minded. And I remembered that a year ago I sat at that table, grumbling the loudest. I'm Arohi, and I didn't like that thought.

qa.q: Which lunch has Arohi stopped going to?
qa.a: The Thursday lunch at the dhaba behind the office.

qa.q: What does Arohi feel when thinking the old friends are small-minded?
qa.a: Arohi feels a superior, distant pride, then an uneasy pang of recognition at having sat at that same table a year ago.

qa.q: What could Arohi do to keep healthy distance without looking down on old friends?
qa.a: Rejoin the lunch now and then, give Manjula an honest, simple answer about the deadline, and keep only truly private things private.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when told not to worry about 'that level'?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt hurt and talked down to by someone who used to share everything with her.

grounding: A new lead skips lunches with old friends, talks down to them and shares less, sliding from natural distance into feeling above them.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Manager's note for Monday's one-to-one with Rukmini
Some observations from the month since Rukmini became shift lead at the call centre.
She no longer takes breaks with her old batch. Ayesha, who trained with her and was her closest friend on the floor, told me she has stopped being invited for evening chai. On Thursday I heard Rukmini tell Ayesha, in front of two new joiners, "Just follow the script, don't try to think," in a tone I haven't heard from her before. Ayesha went quiet and redid the call.
Rukmini has also stopped sharing the weekly targets with the team, passing on only the numbers she thinks they need.
Some distance is normal when someone moves up, and I told her so when she started. This looks like more than distance. On Monday I'll ask her how the role feels, tell her plainly what I saw, and suggest she restart the team huddle she used to love.

qa.q: What did Rukmini tell Ayesha in front of the new joiners?
qa.a: Just follow the script, don't try to think.

qa.q: What might Rukmini be feeling in her new role to act this way?
qa.a: She may feel superior and a little anxious to prove her authority, which comes out as coldness toward old friends.

qa.q: What does the manager plan, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Asking how the role feels, naming exactly what was seen and suggesting she restart the huddle gives her a chance to correct course.

qa.q: How is Ayesha affected by Rukmini's change?
qa.a: Ayesha feels hurt and humiliated, left out of chai and spoken down to in front of new joiners by her closest friend.

grounding: A manager notes a new shift lead who stops taking breaks with old friends, talks down to them and shares less.

passage:
Friday, late
Rashmi messaged again: "Coming for lunch at the canteen? Everyone's asking where you disappeared to 🙂" I said I had a call. I didn't. I ate at my desk and read the quarterly deck instead. Lunch with them is just gossip now, and they don't get what I'm dealing with.
In the afternoon Rashmi asked why her leave was rejected. I explained it slowly, like to a child, and she said, "I know how leave works, Nandini." Fine. Touchy.
I didn't tell the team about the reorganisation rumour, even though I used to tell Rashmi everything first. They don't need to know. Knowing first is part of the job now, isn't it?
Still, when I walked past the canteen at two and heard them laughing, something twisted in my stomach. I told myself I've just outgrown it.

qa.q: What reason did Nandini give Rashmi for skipping lunch?
qa.a: I had a call.

qa.q: What does the twist in Nandini's stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests loneliness and a pang of guilt beneath the story of having outgrown old friends.

qa.q: What could Nandini try before the gap widens?
qa.a: Accept the next lunch invite, apologise to Rashmi for the tone about leave, and share news with the team where possible.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Nandini's new behaviour?
qa.a: Rashmi likely feels hurt and pushed away, talked down to by someone who used to tell her everything first.

grounding: A new lead skips lunches, talks down to an old friend and keeps news back, telling themself they have simply outgrown the group.
